v.why: If edge 2 is already none, removing edge 1 leaves node 2 with no input, so edge 5 carries nothing and the cell loses capacity (exps 50, 52 versus 49, 51).
If edge 1 is already none, removing edge 2 leaves node 2 with no input, so edge 5 is dead; otherwise node 2 still gets input from edge 1.
With edge 1 none, removing edge 0 leaves both node 1 and node 2 with no input, so only edge 3 reaches the output (exps 18, 19 versus 15-17).
With edge 4 already none, removing edge 5 leaves edge 3 as the only input to the output (exp 99 versus 98).
With edge 5 already none, removing edge 4 leaves edge 3 as the only input to the output, so all deep processing is lost.
When edge 4 is none, removing edge 3 makes the output depend only on node 2, so the cell can become nearly disconnected (exp 39).
When edge 5 is none, removing edge 3 leaves only edge 4, a single input to the output, which hurts badly (exp 39 versus 38, 41).
Turning a missing edge 0 into a skip connection gives node 1 an input again, which revives edges 2 and 4 (exp 48), a much bigger gain than replacing a convolution with skip (exp 44).
Replacing a parameter-free pooling on edge 5 with a 3x3 convolution adds learnable capacity at the output, which helps more than replacing a skip connection (exps 5, 6 versus 1-4).
Replacing the 3x3 convolution on edge 5 with pooling throws away the main learnable path into the output, which hurts more than replacing a skip connection (exps 32, 34, 35 versus 33).

That leaves the cell with fewer usable routes, which is consistent with the very large drops in the data (for example #39, #52, #99).

The first-ranked hypothesis is about refilling an empty edge, and two are about swapping between a pooling and a convolution operation on edge 5.
